description: Width tiers for Mathematics Year 1 — ACARA v9. One entry per descriptor code.
subject: Mathematics

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest context or activity that honestly satisfies the descriptor's command term. Every student in the class must reach this floor.
width_notes.typical_width: Full descriptor scope as ACARA intended — grounded in the most common elaboration cases. What a well-taught Year 1 class would have engaged with.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions adding new phenomena, contexts or cultural perspectives. Each item broadens range, not difficulty. 2–4 discrete directions per descriptor.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations are source data for width tiers, not a required checklist. They ground typical_width and identify wider directions including First Nations contexts.

AC9M1N01.minimum_width: Read, write and order two-digit numbers to at least 99 using a number line or chart; recognise and name numerals that look or sound similar (e.g. 16 and 61).
AC9M1N01.typical_width: Read, write, name and order numbers to at least 120 using number lines, hundreds charts and physical materials; use patterns in the number system to read two-digit numbers beyond 20; recognise numbers represented in other languages/cultures (e.g. kanji, Chinese characters); position numbered cards on an empty number line.
wider: Explore how numbers are represented in different cultural and linguistic systems — including Japanese and Chinese numeration — identifying structural similarities and differences with the Hindu-Arabic system.
Investigate First Nations Australians' number languages and oral counting systems, comparing how different language groups represent quantities and order.
Extend the number line to 200 or beyond, predicting and checking what comes next using patterns identified in the hundreds chart.
Use digital tools (virtual hundreds charts, interactive number lines) to explore number order and identify patterns across decades.
elaborations: reading, writing and naming numerals and ordering two-digit numbers from zero to at least 120, using patterns within the natural number system, including numbers that look and sound similar; for example, 16, 60, 61 and 66
using number tracks or positioning a set of numbered cards in the correct order and relative location by pegging on an empty number line

using hundreds charts to build understanding and fluency with numbers; for example, collaboratively building a hundreds chart using cards numbered from zero to 99; colour code the count of tens in a hundreds chart using one colour to represent the number of tens and another to represent the number of ones

recognising that numbers are used in all languages and cultures but may be represented differently in words and symbols; for example, through kanji numbers in Japanese and characters in Chinese, and that there are alternate numeration systems

AC9M1N02.minimum_width: Partition a two-digit number into tens and ones using physical materials; represent at least one alternative partition (e.g. 24 = 10 + 14).
AC9M1N02.typical_width: Partition one- and two-digit numbers in multiple ways using physical and virtual materials; use ten-frames and part-part-whole materials to identify pairs that combine to make 10; partition two-digit numbers into tens and ones and into non-standard groupings; record partitions using numbers.
wider: Investigate how partitioning strategies are represented visually in different ways — ten-frames, bead strings, place-value charts — and compare how each representation makes the structure of the number visible.
Explore partitioning in story and game contexts that reflect a range of cultural counting practices, including grouping strategies used in First Nations counting games.
Use virtual apps to partition numbers to 20 in as many ways as possible, recording and comparing the full set of part-part-whole combinations systematically.
elaborations: building knowledge and understanding of the part-part-whole facts to 10, using physical and virtual materials; for example, using virtual ten-frames through a digital app or website to identify pairs of numbers that combine to make 10
using physical and virtual materials to partition numbers into counts of tens and ones; for example, recognise 35 as 3 tens and 5 ones or as 2 tens and 15 ones

using part-part-whole reasoning and physical or virtual materials to represent 24, then partitioning 24 in different ways and recording the partitions using numbers; for example, 10, 10 and 4 combine to make 24 or 10 and 14 combine to make 24

AC9M1N03.minimum_width: Count a collection of at least 20 objects by grouping into tens and skip counting; connect the digits in the result to the groups counted.
AC9M1N03.typical_width: Count collections of at least 120 objects by grouping into fives or tens and skip counting; connect digits to grouped materials; apply to real contexts including coins; record totals and explain the grouping strategy used.
wider: Compare the efficiency of different grouping sizes (2s, 5s, 10s) for counting large collections, explaining why grouping by 10 connects most directly to the number system.
Count collections using First Nations grouping and tally strategies, exploring how different cultures have approached the challenge of counting large quantities.
Apply skip-counting strategies to count quantities in practical school contexts — books on a shelf, tiles on a floor — and estimate before counting to build number sense.
elaborations: counting a large collection of items using groups of fives or tens and skip counting to work out how many there are; recording the amount and connecting the digits in the number to the grouped materials when using groups of 10

counting collections of objects such as pencils or images of birds in a tree, by grouping them in tens to enable efficient counting and connecting the digits in the number to the groups of tens and ones
counting a large collection of Australian $1 coins by stacking them into piles of 10, skip counting in tens and including any leftover coins to determine the total value

AC9M1N04.minimum_width: Add and subtract within 20 using physical materials and at least one strategy beyond counting all (e.g. counting on, known facts to 10).
AC9M1N04.typical_width: Add and subtract within 20 using a range of strategies — counting on, counting back, partitioning, part-part-whole knowledge to 10, bridging to 10; represent story problems using Think Boards; use + and − symbols and the equal sign; connect materials to symbolic recording.
wider: Create and perform addition and subtraction stories through movement, dance or drama, including stories inspired by First Nations Australians' dances.
Explore addition and subtraction in money contexts using play coins and notes, connecting part-part-whole reasoning to everyday financial situations.
Investigate subitising patterns with dot cards and ten-frames, building fluency with number combinations as a foundation for mental strategies.
elaborations: using drawings, physical and virtual materials and number combinations within 10 to add and subtract collections to 20

adding and subtracting numbers within 20, using a variety of representations and strategies such as counting on, counting back, partitioning and part-part-whole knowledge of numbers to 10; for example, using partitioning and combining 7+5=7+3+2=10+2=12
developing and using strategies for one-digit addition and subtraction based on part-part-whole relationships for each of the numbers to 10 and subitising with physical and virtual materials
representing story problems involving addition and subtraction of numbers within 20 using a Think Board, recognising and using + and – symbols and the equal sign
creating and performing addition and subtraction stories told through First Nations Australians' dances

AC9M1N05.minimum_width: Use mathematical modelling to represent and solve one additive story problem using diagrams or physical materials; explain the connection between the representation and the calculation.
AC9M1N05.typical_width: Model a variety of additive situations (joining, separating, comparing) using Think Boards, diagrams and physical/virtual materials; include simple money transactions in whole dollar amounts; use calculation strategies; explain connections between representation and solution.
wider: Model and solve additive problems set in a range of real-world contexts — bus passengers, lift occupancy, market stalls — choosing appropriate representations for each.
Explore modelling problems involving First Nations Australians' contexts, such as grouping and sharing in community scenarios or counting objects significant to Country/Place.

Investigate how the same additive situation can be represented in multiple ways (number line, part-part-whole diagram, concrete materials) and discuss which representation is clearest for each problem type.
elaborations: modelling problems involving addition and subtraction presented in stories, using a Think Board to represent the problem, solving the problem using physical materials and explaining the connections between any materials used, the Think Board diagram and the numbers within the story
modelling simple money problems involving addition and subtraction using whole dollar amounts; for example, setting up a shop and role-playing practical problems of buying and selling of goods
modelling a variety of different additive situations to solve practical problems; for example, keeping track of the number of people on a bus as it stops to pick up and drop off passengers

AC9M1N06.minimum_width: Model one equal sharing or equal grouping problem using physical materials; represent the result and check that groups are equal.
AC9M1N06.typical_width: Model a variety of equal sharing and equal grouping situations using diagrams and physical/virtual materials; include money contexts (sharing coins equally); use subitising and counting to verify equal groups; record results with numbers.
wider: Model equal sharing and grouping problems across a range of contexts — food, sport, games, community activities — including contexts drawn from First Nations Australians' community practices.
Connect equal grouping to early multiplicative thinking by representing the same situation as a repeated addition and as an equal-groups diagram, comparing the two representations.
Investigate sharing and grouping with remainders (informal) — exploring what happens when objects cannot be shared equally and how to describe the outcome.
elaborations: modelling problems involving repeated equal group situations, such as, 'How many wheels are needed for 3 cars?', using materials and drawing a picture to show what they did
modelling practical problems involving equal sharing situations; for example, sharing a set of dominoes between the 2 players in a game
modelling money problems involving equal sharing; for example, sorting coins from a money box according to their denominations, sharing the coins equally between 4 people

AC9M1A01.minimum_width: Recognise and continue a skip counting sequence by twos, fives or tens starting from zero; identify the rule being used.
AC9M1A01.typical_width: Recognise, continue and create skip counting sequences by twos, fives and tens using number charts, songs, objects and materials; identify digit patterns in skip counting sequences (e.g. fives always end in 0 or 5); apply skip counting to count coins of the same denomination.
wider: Explore skip counting sequences in different cultural contexts — including the Korean counting game Sam-yuk-gu — comparing how pattern rules operate across different representations.
Investigate First Nations Australians' counting traditions and sequences, identifying pattern structures and comparing them with skip counting sequences in the decimal system.
Create visual representations of skip counting sequences using block or bead models, connecting the growing pattern to its numerical sequence and predicting future terms.
Apply skip counting to practical packing and assembly contexts (role-play), reasoning about totals without counting individually.
elaborations: using number charts, songs, rhymes and stories to establish skip counting sequences of twos, fives and tens
using shapes and objects to represent a growing pattern formed by skip counting
recognising the patterns in sequences formed by skip counting; for example, that skip counting in fives starting from zero always results in either a 5 or zero as the final digit
counting by twos, fives, or tens to determine how much money is in a collection of coins or notes of the same denomination
role-playing being an industrial robot on an assembly line that packs various items into boxes or packets in groups of five or ten
using different variations of the popular Korean counting game Sam-yuk-gu for generating skip counting pattern sequences

AC9M1A02.minimum_width: Recognise the repeating unit in a given repeating pattern and continue the pattern; describe the unit of repeat.
AC9M1A02.typical_width: Recognise, continue and create repeating patterns using numbers, symbols, shapes and objects; identify the unit of repeat and represent it using letters or symbols (e.g. SSCSC); recognise repeating patterns in the natural number sequence (0–9 digit repeat within decades); use dynamic geometric software or generative AI to create repeating patterns.
wider: Investigate repeating patterns in First Nations Australians' counting systems and oral/gestural number representations, comparing how the unit of repeat functions across different number languages.

Explore repeating patterns in First Nations Australians' craft practices — such as shell or seed necklace making — recognising how sorting and sequencing decisions create mathematical pattern structures.
Create repeating patterns using a digital generative tool, articulating the instructions needed to produce the pattern and testing whether variations produce the expected result.
Investigate repeating patterns across different media — textiles, music, architecture — identifying the unit of repeat and representing it abstractly.
elaborations: interpreting a repeating pattern sequence created by someone else, noticing and describing the repeating part of the pattern and explaining how they know what comes next
generalising a repeating pattern by identifying the unit of repeat and representing the elements using numbers, letters or symbols
recognising within the sequencing of natural numbers that 0–9 digits are repeated both in and between the decades
collaboratively creating a repeating geometric pattern using dynamic geometric software or a generative artificial intelligence tool
identifying the repeating patterns in First Nations Australians' systems of counting, exploring different ways of representing numbers including oral and gestural language

considering how the making of shell or seed necklaces by First Nations Australians' includes practices such as sorting shells and beads based on colour, size and shape, and creating a repeating pattern sequence

AC9M1M01.minimum_width: Directly compare two or three objects using one attribute (length, mass or capacity); order them and communicate the reasoning using comparative language.
AC9M1M01.typical_width: Compare directly and indirectly and order objects and events using length (string method), mass (hefting and balance scales), capacity (pouring) and duration (sand timers); use and explain correct comparative language (shortest/longest, lightest/heaviest, least/most, faster/slower); communicate reasoning about the order.
wider: Investigate measurement contexts from First Nations Australians' knowledge — including estimating duration of seasons, reading animal track lengths, and water management techniques using traditional vessels and rock holes — comparing these measurement practices with familiar school contexts.
Explore indirect comparison strategies for measuring distance and height using a range of mediating materials (rope, ribbon, body parts), discussing why the choice of mediating material matters.
Compare and order the duration of classroom routines and events using informal timers, constructing a visual timeline and explaining the order.
elaborations: using a piece of string to indirectly compare the length of several objects, deciding which will fit within a space; using comparative language to describe the order: shortest, short, longer, longest
ordering the mass of 3 or more objects such as rocks, using hefting and balance scales; using comparative language to explain the order: lightest, light, heavier, heaviest
pouring sand/rice/water from one container to another to compare and order the capacity of 3 or more containers
creating sand timers from everyday items or recycled material and comparing them to order the duration of time

investigating situations where First Nations Australians estimate, compare and communicate measurements; for example, the duration of seasons; understanding animal behaviour using the length of animal tracks; investigating capacity through water management techniques

AC9M1M02.minimum_width: Measure the length of one object using a uniform informal unit placed end-to-end; count the units and record the result.
AC9M1M02.typical_width: Measure lengths of several objects using a uniform informal unit (blocks, pop sticks, pencils) placed end-to-end without gaps or overlaps; compare two objects by measuring and state which is longer and by how much; explain why the unit must be uniform; use footsteps to measure distances and explain variation in results.
wider: Compare measurements of the same object using two different informal units, explaining why different units give different counts and what this reveals about the relationship between unit size and measurement.

Investigate how body-based measurement units (handspans, footsteps, cubits) have been used historically and by First Nations Australians, comparing these to uniform units and discussing why uniformity matters for communication.

Measure and compare features of the classroom environment (door width, desk length, corridor distance) using chosen informal units, recording findings and discussing whether results are easy to compare across groups.
elaborations: using 2 different units; for example, pop sticks and pencils, to measure the length of an object such as a desk, and explaining why the number of units used may be different
comparing the length of 2 objects by laying multiple copies of a unit and counting to say which is longer and how much longer; explaining why there shouldn't be gaps or overlaps
measuring the distance between 2 locations using footsteps, comparing the results and explaining why there may be different results
measuring and comparing the length of objects using blocks, comparing the height of 2 toys by stacking blocks

AC9M1M03.minimum_width: Name at least four familiar time units (hours, days, weeks, years) and sequence two or three familiar events using these units.
AC9M1M03.typical_width: Name and use years, months, weeks, days and hours; compare the number of days in months and explain the annual cycle; sequence familiar events including using pictorial timelines; reason about whether activities take an hour, day, week, month or year; connect time units to personal experience.
wider: Investigate First Nations Australians' seasonal calendars and how duration and sequence of events are represented across different language groups, comparing these representations with monthly/weekly calendar conventions.
Create a personal or class pictorial timeline spanning a school term, sequencing events and annotating with appropriate time units, discussing how far apart events are.
Explore time duration through comparing natural phenomena — how long does a plant grow, how long do different animals sleep — using months, weeks and days.
elaborations: naming, listing and using familiar units of time, such as hours, days, weeks, years
comparing the number of days in the months of the year and explaining how the months cycle from one year to the next
sequencing familiar events including the representation of time with pictorial timelines
discussing events and activities and deciding whether they would take closer to an hour, a day, a week, a month or a year
investigating durations of time represented in First Nations Australians' seasonal calendars

AC9M1SP01.minimum_width: Classify a collection of shapes into groups; state at least one similarity within a group and one difference between groups.
AC9M1SP01.typical_width: Make, compare and classify familiar shapes including circles, ovals, triangles, quadrilaterals and irregular shapes; identify similarities and differences between groups; recognise familiar shapes and objects in the environment; describe shapes by feel (tactile identification); compare 3D objects built from the same number of blocks.
wider: Explore string games used in storytelling by First Nations Australians — such as Karda from the Yandruwandha Peoples — recognising, comparing and classifying the shapes made by the string and connecting them to shapes found on Country/Place.
Investigate shapes found in architecture, art and the natural environment across different cultural contexts, classifying and comparing properties systematically.
Use dynamic geometry software to create, transform and compare shapes, exploring how changing one property affects classification.
elaborations: classifying a collection of shapes, including different circles, ovals, regular and irregular shapes, triangles and quadrilaterals, saying what is the same about the shapes in a group and what is different between the groups
selecting a shape from a small collection of shapes inside a bag and describing the shape by feel, so that others can name the shape and give reasons for their choice
comparing the different objects that can be built out of the same number of blocks or centi-cubes and discussing the differences between them

exploring string games used in story telling by First Nations Australians; for example, Karda from the Yandruwandha Peoples, recognising, comparing, describing and classifying the shapes made by the string and their relationship to shapes and objects on Country/Place

AC9M1SP02.minimum_width: Follow a sequence of directions to move from one location to another within a familiar space, using at least two directional terms correctly.
AC9M1SP02.typical_width: Give and follow multi-step directions using forwards/backwards, straight ahead, left/right and ordinal language; create and follow an algorithm of step-by-step instructions to move an object; role-play robot movement following and giving instructions; use directional language to describe position within a line.
wider: Describe a familiar journey across Country/Place using directional language from a First Nations perspective, recognising how directions are contextualised by landmark and relationship to Country.
Program a floor robot (Bee-Bot or equivalent) using a sequence of direction instructions, testing and debugging the algorithm to reach a target location.
Create and exchange direction puzzles with peers — one student writes instructions, another follows them — evaluating whether the instructions were precise enough to reach the intended destination.
elaborations: interpreting and following directions around familiar locations, using words like 'forwards' and 'backwards', 'straight ahead', 'left or right' to describe movement
creating and following an algorithm consisting of a set of instructions to move an object to a different location; for example, role-playing being a robot and following step-by-step instructions
following directions to move people into different positions within a line using both ordinal and positional language
describing a familiar journey across Country/Place using directional language

AC9M1ST01.minimum_width: Choose a data collection method and record data for one categorical question using at least one recording format (list, tally, drawings or objects).
AC9M1ST01.typical_width: Discuss and try out methods for collecting data on a class question; record data using multiple formats — lists, tally marks, objects, images, stickers, emojis; review collected data and explain what it shows and how the collection method worked; use digital tools where appropriate.
wider: Explore ways of representing, sharing and communicating data through stories and symbols used by First Nations Australians, comparing these systems with conventional tally and list methods.
Role-play a chatbot asking yes/no questions to collect and categorise data, representing results using virtual manipulatives and discussing how the categories were chosen.
Design and carry out a data collection investigation on a self-chosen question of interest to the class, selecting from a range of recording methods and reflecting on effectiveness.
elaborations: discussing methods of collecting data to answer a question, sharing ideas and trying out some of the suggested methods; reviewing the data collected
collecting and recording information on a topic of interest using lists; examining the data to generate some questions that it could answer
creating a tally to record data while observing events such as the year level of students using the bike shed
using star charts with stickers or emojis to represent class data
role-playing being a chatbot asking simple yes/no questions and collecting data, representing using virtual manipulatives
exploring ways of representing, sharing and communicating data through stories and symbols used by First Nations Australians

AC9M1ST02.minimum_width: Represent data in a one-to-one display (pictograph or object display) for one categorical variable; state which category has the most or fewest.
AC9M1ST02.typical_width: Create one-to-one pictographs and object displays; translate data between list/tally and pictograph formats; use skip counting (by fives) to compare frequencies; describe displays including what the categories show and what patterns emerge; discuss zero-frequency categories and how to handle them.
wider: Explore First Nations Australian children's instructive games — such as Kolap from Mer Island — recording outcomes, representing the data in one-to-one displays and discussing patterns in the results.
Collect data from a class investigation and represent it using a digital tool, comparing the digital display with a hand-drawn display and discussing what each format communicates clearly.
Investigate data displays from other year levels or community sources, interpreting the frequencies and discussing what questions the data answers.
elaborations: creating a pictograph with objects or drawings; discussing the possible categories, arranging the objects or drawings, then reflecting on whether the chosen categories were helpful
translating data from a list or pictorial display into a tally chart to make counting easier; using skip counting by fives to compare the numbers within each category
recognising that when there is no data for a particular category you may choose whether or not to include it
representing data with objects and drawings where one object or drawing represents one data value; describing the displays and explaining patterns using counting strategies
discussing what data frequency means in terms of the total count for a particular category
exploring First Nations Australian children's instructive games; for example, Kolap from Mer Island, recording the outcomes, representing and discussing the results
